<summary>The author likens his modest dedication to the ancient religious practice of offering first-fruits, acknowledging that his words are a mere fraction of what the patron's vast virtues deserve. # DOCTOR CONSTANTINE L'EMPEREUR
## of Opwijk,
### *To the Most Illustrious Count*
# MAURICE OF NASSAU
->Councilor to the Governor of<-
->the West Indies, etc.<-
<note>Maurice of Nassau, specifically Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen (1604–1679), was the governor of the Dutch possessions in Brazil, then known as the "West Indies."</note>

*Dawn herself worships and stands in awe of your name,*
*And the wild Indian is amazed by the Western waters,*
<note>original: "Barbarus Indus." In the 17th century, "Indus" was a general term for the indigenous peoples of the Americas (the West Indies).</note>
*And Count Maurice, the shining image of virtues,*
*Wished you also to be present at his councils:*
*This praise is not enough; unless you also deserve Heaven,*
<note>original: "Olympum," the home of the gods in classical myth, used here as a poetic synonym for the Christian Heaven.</note>
*While you restore the sacred scepters of the Idumaean race;*
<note>original: "Gentis Idumææ." This refers to the region of Edom/Judea; Constantine L'Empereur was a famous scholar of Hebrew and Jewish history, and this line celebrates his work in "restoring" ancient Jewish history through his translations.</note>
*Behold, the high palaces of heaven applaud you,*
*Nor does your fame remain trapped in an earthly prison.*
*To have pleased the gods of this world is no small praise,*
*But the greatest is to be able to please the celestial God.*

# LORD CONSTANTIJN L'EMPEREUR
## of Opwijck,
### *To the Most Illustrious Count*
# MAURICE OF NASSAU
### Counselor to the Governor
### of the West Indies <note>Referring to Dutch Brazil, where Maurice of Nassau served as Governor-General from 1637 to 1644.</note>, etc.

*The Dawn herself <note>A poetic reference to the East.</note> venerates and dreads your name,*
*And the uncivilized Indian stands amazed by the Western waters,*
*And Count Maurice, a shining image of all virtues,*
*Desired that you also be present at his councils:*
*Yet this praise is not enough, unless you also win over Heaven,*
*While you bring back the sacred scepters of the Idumæan race <term>Idumæan: Poetic Latin for Judean or Jewish; refers to L’Empereur’s academic work in translating and "restoring" ancient Hebrew texts for a Christian audience</term>;*
*Behold, the high palaces of heaven applaud you,*
*Nor does your fame remain trapped within an earthly prison.*
*To have pleased the gods of this world <note>Referring to powerful earthly rulers like Maurice of Nassau.</note> is no small praise,*
*But the greatest achievement is to be able to please the celestial God.*

->ANTONIUS THYSIUS, Jurist<- <note>Antonius Thysius (1603–1665) was a noted Dutch historian and legal scholar at the University of Leiden.</note>

<summary>A dedicatory poem by Antonius Thysius honoring the scholar Constantijn L'Empereur for his appointment as a counselor to Maurice of Nassau and for his significant contributions to Hebrew scholarship.</summary>

...[Hebre]ws' Senate, specifically the **Seventy** <note>The Great Sanhedrin, the supreme legal and religious assembly of seventy-one elders in ancient Israel</note>, shared the "power of the sword"—that is, the authority to punish by death—with the **Twenty-Three** capital judges. ### CHAPTER XVI.

### *Concerning the Ecclesiastical Polity of the ten tribes.*

The **Ecclesiastical Polity** <term>the organizational structure and government of a religious body</term> among the **ten tribes** <note>The Northern Kingdom of Israel, which split from the Southern Kingdom of Judah after the death of King Solomon</note> was far more disordered than the **Civil** [polity], on account of the **Idolatry** which the Kings themselves introduced. This was done specifically so that the people—who were otherwise religious (or at least superstitious)—would not return to **Jerusalem**, and eventually turn back to the **kings of Judah**. Nevertheless, this [polity] can be divided in two parts: namely, into the **Pious** and the **Idolatrous**. The **Idolatrous** [polity] (just as **Satan is the ape of God** <note>original: *Satan simia Dei*; a common historical theological proverb suggesting that evil mimics the forms of divine worship to deceive the faithful</note>) was fashioned according to the model of the genuine one; except that

->**THE JEWISH REPUBLIC**<-

Bb 2

**Page 138. [That] those judges had come to Jerusalem]** There is no difficulty here that would require us to resort to one interpretation or the other; indeed, both would contradict the king’s original establishment, since they ought to have administered the law in their own city. Therefore, **Second Chronicles 19:8** should be translated simply as: *wa-yashuvu* <note>Hebrew: וישובו</note>, **"after they had returned."** The sense of the passage is this: Jehoshaphat had set out to the other cities in order to lead the people back to the true religion (**verse 4**) — an act which, as is clear from **Second Chronicles 17:7, 8, and 9**, he was able to accomplish through the agency of others — and to restore the system of justice. Once he himself had **returned to Jerusalem** along with those **civil and religious** <note>original Latin: *politicis & ecclesiasticis*</note> officials, it was only then that he finally appointed judges within Jerusalem itself. In this manner, that **vav** <note>The Hebrew letter ו, which usually means "and," but can also indicate a sequence of time or a result.</note> is used elsewhere...

<note>The following is a quote from the Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:3, provided in the original Hebrew and then Latin.</note>
Antigonus of Soho used to say: "Do not be like servants who serve their master on the condition of receiving a reward; but be like servants who serve their master without the condition of receiving a reward, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you." <note>original Hebrew: *Antigonus ish Soho...*</note> **Antigonus of Soho** <note>a prominent Jewish teacher in the 3rd century BCE</note> was accustomed to say, **"Do not be like servants who minister to their master on the condition that they receive a payment; but be like servants ministering to the master without the condition of receiving payment: indeed, let the reverence of God rest upon you."**

From this, **Antigonus’s** disciple **Zadok** and his fellow disciple **Boethus** <note>original: *Baithos*; according to Jewish tradition, these two students misinterpreted Antigonus’s teaching to mean there was no reward after death, leading to the formation of the Sadducean and Boethusian sects</note> seem to have drawn their error, or rather their voluntary heresy:

*...so that they recognized neither angel nor any spirit—that is, whether of man or of angel—and consequently, not even the resurrection, just as we read in Acts 23:8.* <note>original: *Actor. 23, 8*. This New Testament passage notes that Sadducees, unlike the Pharisees, did not believe in the resurrection or spirits.</note> *For if no reward* <note>original: *merces*; meaning a divine payment or retribution for deeds done in life</note> *is to be hoped for, what good is the resurrection? If even the spirit of man remained after death, a reward would be given at least to the surviving soul, which their teacher Antigonus seemed to have denied. Furthermore, they believed that the soul and the angel, because of their similarity, were subject to the same logic. But truly, the mind of **Antigonus of Soho** was far different. His own words allow for two suitable interpretations.*

**The first way is that "reward"** <note>original Hebrew: *peras*; a term for a gift or payment</note> **always refers to physical repayment in this world, and it is never used in any context to refer to the reward of the soul.**

<page-num>445</page-num>

**However, "reward" is sometimes used for physical compensation, and many times it is used for spiritual compensation.** <note>original Hebrew: אמנם השכר נאמר פעם על הגמול הגשמי ופעמים רבות יאמר על הגמול הנפשיי. The author is quoting a Hebrew source to distinguish between *sachar* (general reward) and *peras* (a specific type of payment).</note> The first method of explaining this (as **Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman, philosopher, and biblical commentator.</note> observes) is that the term *Peras* <note>original Hebrew: *peras*; a term often used for a discretionary gift or a portion of a payment rather than a legally mandated wage.</note> is always used for physical compensation in this world, and truly is not used in any way for spiritual reward; but the term **reward** <note>original: *merces*; here translating the Hebrew *sachar*</note> is sometimes used for physical payment, and is often used for a spiritual reward. Therefore, in this matter, **Zadok** deviated from his teacher’s intention by claiming that all reward was being denied; whereas his teacher [Antigonus] had only exhorted his students not to devote themselves to good works for the sake of this life's rewards, but rather for the life to come. This point can be confirmed by the words of **Rabbi Abraham** in *the Tradition* <note>original: *R. Abrahami in Kabala*; this refers to Abraham ibn Daud (c. 1110–1180) and his work *Sefer ha-Qabbalah* (The Book of Tradition), which traces the history of Jewish oral law to refute the Karaites.</note>.

**The shifts of the priestly divisions.** 133. <note>Latin: *Turmarum vices*. This refers to the rotating schedule (courses) by which different groups of priests and Levites served in the Temple throughout the year.</note>

### V.

**The right of the elders over the family.** 38.
**The necessity of anointing.** 251 and 419. <note>The ritual of pouring sacred oil upon a person to designate them for a holy office, such as a king or high priest.</note>
**The deputy commander in Jerusalem.** 164. <note>original Greek: "ὑποστράτηγος ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις" (*hypostratēgos en Hierosolymois*). This refers to a military or administrative official under a higher governor.</note>
**Designation of the cities of refuge,** 241. **and those assigned to the Levites.** 242. <note>The Cities of Refuge were six towns in the Kingdom of Israel and Judah where those who committed accidental manslaughter could claim asylum from blood vengeance.</note>
**The civil administration in the time of King Uzziah.** 286. <note>Uzziah was a long-reigning king of Judah known for his military reforms and agricultural advancements.</note>
**The office of the Uzzielites.** 275. <note>A clan of Levites descended from Uzziel, the uncle of Moses; they performed specific duties in the care of the Tabernacle.</note>

### Z.

**The office of Zebadiah.** 140. <note>Several men named Zebadiah appear in the biblical record, often serving as judicial or military officials under kings like Jehoshaphat.</note>
**The sect of the Zealots, their destruction.** 344 following, 449 and following. <note>The Zealots were a radical political and religious movement in 1st-century Judea that incited the rebellion against the Roman Empire, leading to the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note>
